AYLESWORTH (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 31) to prevent the payment or acceptance of illicit or secret commissions and other like practices. He said the object of this legislation is fairly well indicated by the title. It is proposed to enact that the payment or acceptance of illicit or secret commissions and practices of that nature shall be an offence punishable either by indictment or upon summary conviction, according to the gravity of the circumstances. The measure is one of general application. We have already upon the statute book, in the shape of sections in the Criminal Code, enactments against the receiving of secret commissions by agents in the employ of any Government in Canada or of any municipal corporation. But this legislation proposes to go further and make it criminal on the part of any employee to accept any secret commission in consideration of favours to be given at the expense of his employer. This legislation is in substance the enactment adopted on the subject by the Imnerial Parliament two years ago. The Bill as drafted is an adaptation of that legislation and simply proposes to adopt, for the purposes of this country the legislation which, in that respect is now on the Statute Book of Great Britain. The clauses of the Criminal Code, to which I have referred, will none the less have their application to transactions within their scope and which may have already taken place. The enactment now proposed will to some extent cover the same ground, and it is proposed to increase the incidence of punishment and to make offences of the general character I have described fall within the provisions of the Act. The Bill consists simnly of a clause defining the terms used in the proposed legislation and one declaring that every one who falls iii
within the description of the proposed statute is guilty of an offence and liable, either upon indictment or summary conviction, to the penalties proposed.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Mr. JOHN BARR (Dufferin) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 32) to amend the Railway Act. He said this Bill is somewhat similar to the one introduced last session. * Its object is to facilitate the crossing of railways by telephones, telegraphs, watermains, viaducts, and so on. The difficulty under the present law is that permission must be asked from the railway company before any such crossing can be made. _ In the rural districts, the railway companies demand $5 for each crossing. In my opinion this is most unjust. If the parties refuse to pay the ?5, they must apply to the railway board. This involves the drawing and filing of plans and the employment of legal counsel and necessitates considerable delay and expense. We know that the railway commission is overworked, and the result is months' delay before the sanction of the board is obtained to any application of the kind. At present telephone companies, small and great, are being built throughout the length and breadth of the country, and are accomplishing considerable good by bringing the rural districts in close communication with the towns and villages; and it is unfortunate that they should be frequently hampered and delayed in their efforts by reason of difficulties and delays in crossing the railway tracks, besides being put to a great deal of expense through having to make application to the railway commission. By adopting this Bill, which provides that the railways cannot demand or receive any compensation from telegraph and telephone companies for the right to cross a railway track, we will relieve the railway board of a good deal of work. Another provision in this Bill is that application may be made to the station master within the jurisdiction, or of the most convenient station master; and if no action be taken by the railway company during fifteen days, the applicants may go on and cross the railway tracks. So far as watermains and viaducts are concerned, they must give fifteen days' notice and pay the expenses of the engineer who will examine the work. If this Bill be carried, it will lessen the work of the railway commission, and relieve the telegraph and telephone and watermata companies from the long delay and expense now unavoidable.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

That in the opinion of this House it is advisable to appoint a select standing committee on natural resources who shall have authority to inquire into and consider and report upon all matters appertaining to the conservation and development of the natural resources of Canada, including fisheries, forests, mines, minerals, waterways and water powers, and to whom may be referred from time to time any report, document or matter touching the subject which they are appointed to consider.

Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have no objection to my hon. friend going on with his motion, but I do not think the government
can close the debate on it to-day.

My remarks will not be very lengthy. So far as the exact wording of this resolution is concerned, I shall be very glad indeed to accept any suggestion from the government or any hon. member of this House. My object is to point out that public interest in the conservation and development of the great natural resources of this country might be stimulated by action of parliament. We have at present a committee on agriculture. That committee has engaged for the most part in thoroughly non-partisan work and work which has been of great advantage to the people. We thoroughly realize that agriculture must be the principal basis upon which the future wealth of this country depends ; but that consideration should not blind us to the further fact that we have, outside of agriculture, in the fisheries, forests, mines, minerals, waterways and waterpowers of this country, very great resources, the extent of which we do not at present realize, and the development and conservation of these are of very great importance to the people.
Now, in speaking of ' development ' and ' conservation ' I believe that these two words should be the watchwords of the country with regard to its natural resources. Conservation does not mean nonuser; on the contrary, it is consistent with that reasonable user of these great resources 'which is absolutely necessary for their development. And, on the other hand, development does not imply destruction or waste; it ought not to imply destruction or waste, but these great resources should be both developed and conserved, so that they may be of the greatest possible advantage to the present generation and may also be handed down as a continuing heritage to those who come after us in the work of upbuilding this Dominion and the British empire.
We have had a great many stimulating addresses throughout the country on the importance of these great resources. One might expect that the parliament of Canada would be one of the great forces in awakening public interest in our resources, and the consideration of means by which the development and conservation of these resources should be carried out. But owing, I believe, to some extent at least, to the fact that we have had no committee of parliament specially charged with the consideration of our natural resources, parliament has not taken the initiative to any very considerable degree, and the stimulus of public interest and public attention in respect of these matters has come to us almost altogether from outside sources. I

do not desire to put out of sight the most excellent work which the Canadian Forestry Association has done in awakening public interest in our forests. Nor do I desire for a moment to put aside consideration of the forestry congress or conference called by the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) some three years ago, which I had the privilege of attending, and which, I think, did very good work in awakening public interest in this matter. I think the Prime Minister, at that time, announced that at some future date a further conference or congress of the same character would be called. I have no doubt that the effect of that meeting was to stimulate public interest and to educate the public in appreciation of these great resources, and in that way to assist the object which we are all interested in accomplishing. Nor do I put to one side the work which has been accomplished by the forestry branch of the Department of the Interior. I know that that branch has been established only a short time ; I know that it has not yet had an opportunity to accomplish the very great work which has been accomplished in the United States of America by the forestry service presided over by Dr. Pinchot. I have had, during the past three or four years, the privilege of receiving from the forestry service of the United States a number of the publications which they issue from time to time. If I brought them all here and laid them on the table of the House-and I do not suppose that I have a complete set-they would make a pile a foot or a foot and a half high. I have brought a few, which will show that these publications are of a most practical, interesting and varied character. An example is one published in 1908, called ' The Use Book,' containing almost a complete manual of the work which the Forestry Service of the United States accomplishes, giving directions of an extremely interesting and useful character to the people who may desire to solicit the co-operation of the United States Forestry Bureau. There are a number of pamphlets of a thoroughly practical character issued to the farmers and others throughout the country. For instance, ' Practical Assistance in Tree Planting,' ' How to Grow Young Trees for Forest Planting,' * How to Transplant Forest Trees,' ' Progress of Forestry, 1905,' 'Forest Planting Leaflet '-these are issued in very great numbers, instructing farmers and others interested how transplanting should be done-' Consumption of Pulpwood in the United States,' ' Lumber Cut of the United States, 1906,' ' Wood Used for Pulp, 1905,' and so on in great variety and giving a vast amount of useful information. I desire it to be thoroughly understood that I refer to this not as casting any reflection on the work of the forestry branch of the Department of the Interior. I believe that the 124
officials engaged in that branch are doing the best they can. They have been engaged in the work only a short time, and, while it is not practicable to go to the Forestry Branch of Canada and obtain all the information that is available to one who consults the publications of the Forest Service of the United States, I have no doubt that that condition is being remedied as rapidly as possible, and that we shall have i-n Canada, in the near future, a Forestry Bureau which will give the same information, the same evidence of active and aggressive work in this connection as is given by the Forestry Service of the United States under the very able presidency of Dr. Pinchot, who spoke in this city not long ago upon these subjects.
I would say, in that connection, that the attention of the people of the United States has been called very thoroughly to the importance not only of the development but of the conservation of their natural resources. I do not know that I can do better, in order to icall the attention and awaken the interest of our own people in this matter, than to quote a few words from the very able and interesting address which Dr. Pinchot delivered in this city on the occasion of his last visit. He came, as I understand it, to bear a message from the President of the United States to His Excellency the Governor General and the right hon. leader of the government inviting the co-operation of this government in a conference or congress to be held in the capital of the United States, the delegates to include not only representatives of the United States, but also representatives of Canada and Mexico, in order that the people of the entire continent, through their accredited representatives, might consider methods of co-operation in this work of conservation of the natural resources of the continent. I do not know when that convention is to be held, but the announcement was made, on behalf of this government on that occasion, that the government of Canada proposed to send representatives to the meeting. I was very glad indeed to hear that announcement, and I am sure that the right hon. Prime Minister and his colleagues may count upon the co-operation of the members on this side in this work which has already been attended with such beneficial effects in the United States. Now, going back to Dr. Pinchot's address, I desire to quote a few words from it. Speaking of the steps taken in the United States towards the conservation and development of their great natural resources, he said:
The appointment of" a waterways commission was the first step. The second was the great convention of governors of States in Washington last May, at which all the States were represented, at which for the first time the attention of the nations was called to the waste going on. The next step was a meeting

of the National Conservation Commission at which the governors of half the States were present and delegates from other States, and at which both the outgoing president and the incoming president attended, and spoke, the latter being the chairman, and committing the new administration thorougliy and confidently to the policy of conservation left by the old administration; so that we know that in the United States, for four years more at least, this attempt to carry over for our children some of the things we received from our forefathers is going to continue. The first piece of work the National Conservation Commission did was to prepare an inventory of the national resources of the country, a somewhat rough and ready one, but so far as 1 know this is the first time that any nation has toted up its balance sheet and attempted to get an approximate knowledge of its supplies of natural resources. In other words, we have taken stock in the ordinary way in which any prudent man takes stock of what he has, so that we may inform ourselves of what we have, because we are to depend mainly upon ourselves for our supply hereafter. We are beginning to realize that; and, like a man cast away in a boat at sea, we are beginning to find out how Jong our water and food will last, and what we ought to do to save them. We learned a great many very striking facts. For example, we discovered (hat a preventable waste in our coal supplies amounts to some $300,000,000 every year; that if we go on increasing the use of them at the present rate, they will probably he gone by the middle of the next century-a long time perhaps, and yet not long in the life of a nation; that our iron supplies, which are just as necessary as our coal-the high grade ores-will be gone by the middle of this century; and that our oil and gas supplies will probably he gone by the middle of this century. We found that our lauds are being washed into the sea at the rate of 800 million cubic tons per year-that our farmers have been losing over $500,000,000 a year from easily preventable soil erosion, $130,000,000 a year from Injurious animals, and two or three times that amount from injurious insects and other forms of preventable waste; that some of our public lands were being disposed of in such ways that the number of homes on the lands were not being increased, which is the real test; that we are cutting out forests three and a half times faster than they are being produced; and that our forests are only growing at the rate of twelve cubic feet per acre per annum when they might easily grow at the rate of forty,-which shows the great loss of wood material that might be made but that is not being made. We found that of every thousand feet of lumber standing in the forests only a little over 300 feet gets into use; that the waste in logging, in milling, in seasoning, in working up afterwards, used up from the standing trees all hut about 310 board feet for every thousand hoard feet standing in the woods. And a very large part of that waste is preventable. We found that the reasonably available water-powers in the country at the present time would move every railroad train, every trolley oar, every wheel and every spindle, light every house, and answer every use of power in the country. That is to say, if our vast supplies of coal were burned up, Mr. E. L. BORDEN.
they might easily to a great extent be replaced by the use of our water-powers which are at present largely going to waste. We found that our water-powers were in process of being monopolized by two or three great companies-that our water-powers, east and west, south and north, were being acquired as rapidly as those wise and far seeing men could get hold of them, and were thus in danger of being monopolized when our coal supplies were either exhausted or so depleted as to have greatly risen in price, in the hands of one of the most far reaching and oppressive monopolies that has ever existed on the face of the earth. In any country where fuel is scarce, as in California after the oil is gone, every source of power, so far as men of science know at present must come from the streams; and when that time comes, every railway train and trolley car will be run by electric power from water, every house lighted and heated, every gallon of water pumped for irrigation, every bit of manufacture, every bit of printing will be done by electric power from water. At every point the average citizen will come into daily contact with the monopoly that controls the water-power if it is allowed to pass beyond the position of government regulation. So that we feel it strongly that one of the great problems of conservation, with us as with you, is to see that our water-powers are kept in a position where they will serve the public and not the great corporations first and the public afterwards. We learned that our navigable streams cover about 26,000 square miles. We spend $500,000,000 on our rivers and harbours and about half of that on our streams; and yet our navigation has declined in spite of this enormous expenditure, and our streams are less navigable than they were fifty years ago because the soil is being washed into .the streams faster than the government is able to dip it out in order to keep the streams in their original condition. How long the present conditions may be expected to continue, and what ought to be done about them, is the question we have to consider.
Now every one of these pregnant statements of Dr. Pinchot seem to have considerable application to Canada as well as to the United States. I would like to say in this connection that in a recent message addressed to Congress by the President of the United States, this language is used in referring to the work done by the National Conservation Commission which has recently met in the city of Washington:
The principle of the community of interest among all our people in the great natural resources runs through the report of the National Conservation Commission and the proceedings of the joint conference. These resources, which form the common basis of our welfare, can be wisely developed, rightly used, and prudently conserved only by the common action of all the people, acting through their representatives in state and nation. Hence the fundamental necessity for co-operation. Without it we shall accomplish but little, and that little badly.
Then he quotes the words of the resolution, which are as follows:

We also especially urge on the Congress of the United States the high desirability of maintaining a national commission on the conservation of the resources of the country, empowered to co-operate with state commissions to the end that every sovereign commonwealth and every section of the country may attain the high degree of prosperity and the sureness of perpetuity naturally arising in the abundant resources and the vigour, intelligence, and patriotism of our people.
Now haying touched upon these inspiring utterances of Dr. Pinchot, which were listened to with the greatest attention and interest by every person present, let me, before dealing very briefly with the various resources such as forests, mines, etc., with which we are endowed in Canada, refer to a very patriotic work which has been done in the province of British Columbia by Mr. A. C. Flumerfelt, who has offered, during the past two or three years, prizes in that province for the best essays upon the potential resources of the province of British Columbia. I daresay that every hon. gentleman in this House has received a copy of the essays, embodied in pamphlet form, which are the results of Mr. Flumer-felt's patriotic endeavours. They contain a vast amount of information with regard to the natural resources of British Columbia, and I do not doubt that when our Canadian forestry bureau gets to work, when possibly some conservation commission is established in this country, we may have pamphlets of this kind with regard to all the natural resources of Canada, for we need them very badly at the present time.
Now, I would like to say to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister of Canada, and I am saying it without casting any discredit upon the government, without casting any discredit upon the forestry bureau which has been recently established, that I have spent, during the last year a great deal of time, first and last, endeavouring to find out only a few things regarding the various resources of Canada. I wanted to find out, in the first place, whether the forest resources of Canada are enormously greater, as, I thought at one time, than the forest resources of the United States ; I wanted to find out what is the total acreage of the land in Canada which we can regard as properly available for the purpose of producing merchantable timber for export or for use at home; I wanted to ascertain how rapidly we are cutting that every year; I desired to ascertain how rapidly it is being replaced by the natural growth of the forest; and I am bound to say that, at the present time, there does not exist in Canada any official information whatever on these points, so far as I am aware, taking the country as a whole. Some information may exist in respect to one of two of the provinces, but taking the Dominion of Canada at the present time, there is absolutely no official information on those heads. I am not saying this in criticism of
the present government or of any previous government, but I am saying it for the purpose of indicating to the Prime Minister, and to my colleagues in parliament, and to the people of this country, the urgent need of thorough and systematic work for the purpose of obtaining this information and placing it before the Canadian people.
1 shall not this afternoon attempt any lengthy dissertation upon the natural resources of Canada. The greatness of the subject. itself would be appalling to any man who would attempt to deal with it exhaustively. Let me speak first of the fisheries. My hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) brought to the attention of parliament last year the importance of having a select standing committee of this House upon the fisheries. At that time I concurred entirely with the view expressed by my hon. friend upon the importance of the fisheries and the necessity of some action by parliament for the purpose of stimulating interest and also bringing about a more efficient operation of the fisheries in this country and better preservation of them for those who are to come after us. The fisheries of the Atlantic and the Pacific coast as well are of very great importance to the people of Canada. I do not believe they are carried on as thoroughly and effectively at present as they might be. I believe that we have on both the Atlantic and the Pacific coasts many species of fish which are not now sought, but which will some day be utilized for food, and I believe also that the fisheries of the Atlantic coast might be made to supply the needs of the people of Quebec ana Ontario to a very much greater extent than at present. This must depend to some extent upon means of transportation and upon better methods by the fishermen and better co-operation among them. I am glad to say that there is to-day more co-operation among the fishermen of the maritime provinces, especially of Nova Scotia than there has been in the past. All these things might be encouraged and stimulated by a committee upon natural resources, because I would suggest that if such a committee be appointed, there should be sub-committees on fisheries, forests, and mines and minerals, each taking up the particular subject assigned to it; in that way such a committee could do a very great deal of work along a line that I believe to be in the public interest, the development and conservation of every one of these great industries.
Coming for a moment to our forests, one realizes that the forests of this country should be and are one of the greatest sources of our national wealth. The subject of forestry has been studied and developed upon scientific and common-sense principles in Europe. Many parts of our own country are unsuitable for agriculture but are eminently suitable for forestry.

Those who are interested in this subject would do well to consult an article of Dr. Fernow in the ' Forest Quarterly ' of December, 1908, from which I propose to quote a little later. Dr. Fernow points out that a very large area indeed, of several of the provinces of Canada can be usefully employed for forestry purposes and for no other purpose.
I shall take but one illustration of many that could be given of the use that is made of mountainous lands in other countries. Saxony has under state control 430,000 acres of rough mountain land-an area not larger than an average county in Canada. From this she has taken two hundred million dollars in the past fifty years. During that time the cut has been doubled and is of infinitely better quality than it was fifty years ago. Then, only 17 per cent of the cut was serviceable, now 79 per cent is serviceable and the standing wood in the state forests has increased by no less than 16 per cent. The gross revenue per acre has increased from $1.75 to $6.67, and the net revenue per acre from 95 cents to $4.37. Canada possesses a forest area at least a thousand times greater than that of Saxony. While I am not advocating a policy of expropriation for the forest lands, nevertheless Canada and the several provinces of Canada do retain under state control an enormous amount of land which can be usefully employed for no other purpose.
There has been an enormous denudation of forest lands in the United States and the people of that country are beginning to realize that the true principle to be applied to forests; is the principle of harvest and not that of destruction of the resources from which the harvest comes. It is estimated that the United States have at the present time 500,000,000 acres of forest lands. The estimates in regard to Canada vary greatly, from 800,000,000 acres to 1,700,000,000 acres. After consultation with a person who has studied the subject and who possesses an official status in this country, I am convinced that the actual area in the United States as well as in Canada available for the purpose of producing merchantable lumber whether for export or for use at home would not exceed 250,000,000 acres in the one country or the other, and I am also convinced notwithstanding the enormous denudation of the forests' in the United States that the United States to-day possesses, contrary to what is generally be lieved, forest reserves slightly greater than those of Canada; and it must further be borne in mind that the forest resources of the United States are being renewed probably more rapidly than those of Canada, because in the southern parts of the United States, where a very considerable portion Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
of their forest area still remains, the growth is probably more rapid than it is in any part of Canada with the possible exception of the maritime provinces. I make this exception because a gentleman who is now engaged in lumbering in Nova Scotia, who has had experience in Sweden, in Scotland, in Newfoundland, in Ontario and in Nova Scotia, tells me. that the spruce forests of Nova Scotia are renewed more rapidly by natural growth than those of any other country in the world.
The paucity of our information in Canada is amazing both as to the extent of resources, area cut, waste and destruction and as to the period for which forests will last under present conditions. Of course when I refer to the present conditions I do not wish to put out of sight the enormous destruction by fire every year. Lumbermen will tell you that if you look over the history of forestry in Canada, an infinitely larger amount of lumber is destroyed by fire than is cut by lumbermen and this very important consideration should engage the attention with the provincial governments to the end that this enormous loss and destruction may be checked, so far as possible, in the future. Very valuable work has been done in the United States by forest patrols. Any one who will examine the reports of Dr. Pinchot, as to what has been done in the United States, particularly in the western portion of the United States, towards guarding against fires will realize that a very great work in this same connection can be carried on in this country, and I believe has been carried to some extent already, so far as our western forests are concerned by the Forestry Branch of the Department of the Interior. I do not, in the slightest, desire to minimize the good work which has been done by that Branch.
A word as to the lumber cut of the United States as compared with that of Canada The lumber cut of the United States, so far as I can obtain any information or details amounts to about 40,000,000,000 every year in merchantable lumber. If you add to that the railway ties, the pulpwood, the cordwood, the fence poles and the other wood that is cut from the forests of the United States, I am informed by Dr. Pinchot, to whom I applied for information on this subject, that the total annual lumber cut of the United States would amount to the equivalent of one hundred thousand million (100,000,000,000) of board measure. We have then to inquire what is the annual destruction of our forests by fire, and what are the total resources of timber in Canada to which we must look if we are concerned as to whether or not the supply will equal the demand in years to come. The best information I have been able to get on this subject is contained in an article by Dr. Fernow, published in the Forestry Quarterly for December, 1908. I wish I could read the whole of this article to the House, but I am afraid it would be too much for me to attempt to place it all on ' Hansard.' I will, however, ask to be allowed to quote two pages of the article because they contain very interesting information and statistics as to what the total forest resources of Canada amount to and where they are situated. Dr. Fernow was at one time head of the Forestry Department of the state of New York, and he is now professor of forestry in the University of Toronto; that university being, I believe, the first in Canada to take the highly commendable step of establishing a school of forestry. Dr. Fernow is reputed to be one of the most reliable authorities on this continent as to the timber resources of Canada and the United States. He has gone into this subject very thoroughly and exhaustively in this article, and if the House will bear with me I will quote a little from it. Speaking of British Columbia and of the western forests generally, he says :
In the mountain mills the average log sawed at the mill is 12 inches, of this description some 15,000,000 acres may be found in the southern Rocky Mountain type, which figured at 5,000,000 feet, gives another 75 billion feet, or altogether for the western Canada forest 300 billion feet. One might easily double these estimates without finding the supply inexhaustible. Every effort is being made to get rid of this valuable limited asset of the province.
Then Dr. Fernow continues:
Taking Ontario alone with a total land area of 126 million acres, of which 80.000,000 are still unsurveyed, we find that the distribution of these lands among three types. of forest country occupied by the province gives 30 million acres to the southern hardwood type, 50 million acres to the central southern Laurentian type, and 46 million acres to the northern forest. Not quite 25 million acres are disposed of to private owners. From the assessment lists we learn, that of these, 14 million acres are cleared, of which 12-4 millions are in the peninsula, Lake Ontario and in St.
acres, nearly 2 million acres are reported as slash, and 2 -8 million as swamp and waste 2:4, 2, and 1 million of the latter respectively in the three sections.
Applying a general experience figure for waste land incapable of recuperation, we would come to the conclusion that 85 million acres or two-thirds of the province will always remain in woods, except so far -as it may be turned into grazing lands.
Mr. Wbitson of the Crown Lands Department, one of the best informed men on these matters, places the figure as at best 70 mil-lieu acres productive forest area, and the stand of pine outside of the licensed lands (12 -5 million acres are licensed, and were some time ago estimated to contain 24 billion feet, the annual out being around 800 million feet) and of forest reserves (10 million acres) at 10 billion feet B. M. and the pulpwood at 288 million cords. He also states that of the jack-pine not 10 per cent is fit even for railroad ties.
For Quebec the distribution of land areas may be made .as follows :-
Of the 218 million acres (342,000 square miles) around 144 million acres belong to the northern forest. 50 million the same amount as for Ontario, to the southern Laurentian: the St. Lawrence valley with 5 million acres represents mostly farm area, and the balance of 19 million acres may be accredited to the Acadian region. There are about 9 million acres in farms, of which 7 -5 millions are in crops, and 1-5 millions is waste land, hence the total forest and waste land area is over 210 million acres. An estimate by Langelier, superintendent of forest rangers, places the standing lumber of the white and red pine at less than 40 billion feet, and spruce saw-logs at over 100 billion, all other saw material (including jackpine) at about 18 billion feet or altogether less than 160 billion feet.
The maritime provinces with somewhat over 57,000 square miles, together with the eastern townships of Quebec, south of the river 130,000 square miles) belong to the Appalachian or Acadian forest type. This area is practically cut out as far as pine is concerned, and irelies now mainly on spruce far saw timber.
In New Brunswick 12 mi.ll/ion acres a.re estimated to be under wood, the composition cf which, by good authorities, is figured at 60 per cent spruce, 10 per cent pine, 5 ner cent hemlock, 5 per cent cedar, 20 per cent hardwoods. Here the larger portion is owned privately, some 10-5 million acres. Of the 7:25 acres of crown lands all but about one million acres is under licenses, the latter area being barrens or burnt.
The small remaining urea of timber land on Prince Edward Island is in calculations like these entirely negligible. New Brunswick. together with No.va Scotia which represents an area of some 14 million acres, may round off the total stand of saw timber in the eastern provinces to 300 billion feet and for the whole of Canada to 600 billion feet. We might readily double these estimates and still remain within reasonable limits of the truth, if a closer utilization, especially on

the Pacific coast, and more careful lumbering generally were practised, and if tile fires running with tolerable regularity through the slash did not destroy much of the growing timber besides the young growth.
I invite the special attention of the House to what he says in conclusion:
Considering that the above estimated stand of saw timber, which others have considerably reduced, would not suffice to supply the present annual consumption of coniferous material in the United States for more than 15 to 20 years, and the import into Great Britain of this class of material for more than 60 to 80 years, the need of securing better knowledge of the conditions of this resource and of employing conservative methods in its use are apparent.
I think every member of this House who has given the subject the slightest consideration will agree with the latter conclusion at which Dr. Fernow has arrived.
Having spoken at this length with regard to the forests, let me say one or two words about the waterways. I regard these as a natural resource. They constituted at one time the only means of communication through the country. At the present time they constitute the cheapest means of communication and of transportation for the carriage of the great products of the country. In so far as the resources of the country will reasonably permit their development, they should be developed-not as political expediency or purely local demands may require, but upon a comprehensive and carefully prepared system based upon the probable future needs of the entire country.
Then, with respect to the water-powers, I am sure that every hon. gentleman who has heard this afternoon the words of Dr. Pin-chot with regard to the importance 'of the water-powers of the United States must be impressed with similar considerations as annlied to Canada. If the water-powers of the United States are so important as he says they are to the people of the United States, I believe that the water-powers of Canada are of infinitely more importance to the people of this country. I believe that their permanence under fair conditions can be assured, and 1 have not much doubt that if properly conserved, these water-powers will prove a more valuable asset to the people of Canada in the future than all our coal and other minerals, all our iron, all our gold and silver combined. They should be investigated, estimated and scheduled. They should not be subject to exploitation for purely individual profit, but should be conserved as an asset held in trust by the state for the benefit of the whole people. I realize that the committee on agriculture and also a committee of the Senate have made some Investigation into matters touching the waterways of Canada.
I believe that a committee such as I sug-Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
gest could do a splendid work along the same lines. That committee could investigate also another subject to which attention has been called by Dr. Pinchot in the portion of his remarks which I quoted this afternoon the destruction of our forests and the consequent denudation of our hills and mountains, which converts our streams into torrents in the spring and dry beds in the summer and early autumn. A great authority in the United States, Professor Shaler, estimated that up to i896 in the upland regions of the states south of Pennsylvania 3,000 square-miles of soil had been destroyed as the result of forest denudation, and that the destruction was then going on at the rate of 100 square miles of fertile soil every year. There cannot be the slightest doubt that the equivalent of hundreds of fertile farms is being washed into the sea every year as the result of our neglect of the proper conservation of our forests.
Our mines are subject to different considerations from the forests and the waterways. The mines must, in the very process of development, eventually become exhausted. But there is good reason, it seems to me, for adopting the view that they should be administered under such a policy as will prevent waste and speculative exploitation, and that, so far as they are not required for immediate operation, the state should retain ownership and control ; and it may be that later on in the history of this country, the state will have to take a step even in advance of what I am now suggesting in that regard.
The question is, what are our resources? At what rate are they being dissipated or wasted ? How can they be developed in the interest of the whole nation ? In view of these considerations, Mr. Speaker, I thought it only right to place upon the Order Paper the motion which is now in your hands. I suggest a committee on natural resources. The work of such a committee could be distributed among subcommittees, and might be made of great service in many ways both to the government and the people. We hear a great deal, both in the United States and in Canada, of the decadence of our legislative institutions, the decadence of the influence of parliament, in these latter days, when almost all the work of government is confined to the members of the Cabinet. I know that that process has gone on in Great Britain, and it is curious to observe that exactly the same development in that respect is to be seen in Canada-that is, the continued decline of the influence of parliament as a parliament, and the continued increase of the oower of the Cabinet. I do not know that that development is a very healthy development, and I suggest to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister that we might perhaps assist in restoring to parliament as a parliament-not as a partisan parliament,

but as a parliament earnestly striving to do some work of value in the public interest-some of its influence. If we could have committees such as the one I suggest, to take into consideration matters of great public interest, matters which perhaps for the time being, in the exigencies of the political situation, could not be taken in hand by the government itself, they might serve a very useful public purpose. The reports of such committees need not be acted upon immediately by the government of the day. For example, I believe that public attention should be directed to the pulp-wood of this country. I realize what the conditions are in Quebec, the maritime provinces and other parts of the country. The people of this country do not understand that at the present time, while our producers are receiving for their pulpwood about $6 or $7 a cord labour bestowed upon it in the United States, when that pulpwood goes across the borders, make it worth $50 or $60 or .$70. I realize that the subject is not free from difficulty ; but it seems to me that a committee of this House, taking up such a matter as that, and bringing before the committee the men who are most strongly opposed to taking any step towards utilizing our pulpwood in our own country, and inviting them to state their, reasons and to argue the matter out, could do a work for the conservation of the national resources of this country which could not be done by the government of the day. So, while men everywhere in Canada are lifting up their voices for the conservation and development [DOT] of our natural resources, it seems to me that some initiative should come from parliament, and that the members of narliament, without regard to party, sinking for this purpose all partisan considerations, should take un this work and endeavour to accomplish somethin? for the good of the country. It is purely in that spirit that I have brought this matter to the attention of the risrht hon. leader of the government and of this House. I am not concerned about the verbiage of the resolutioh, or whether the committee * shall be appointed on the motion of an hon. member on this side of the House or an hon. member on the other side. But I would like to see something done, and I trust that the suggestion that I have taken the liberty of submitting to the consideration of the House will receive the favourable consideration of the Prime Minister and his colleagues and of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, and that in some manner it will be acted upon during the present session.
of Canada,' one is led in these days to consider mainly our water-powers and timber resources, and I listened with great interest to the remarks of the hon. the leader of the opposition in that connection. Though I have not given these two matters sufficient personal attention to hope to contribute anything of interest to the debate, there are a couple of points to which I wish very briefly to refer. My hon. friend referred to the fact that last session the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) proposed that a select committee should be named to deal with matters relating to Marine and Fisheries, and I notice by the Order Paper that that hon. gentleman has given notice of his intention to renew his resolution of last year. In my judgment there is a considerable contrast between matters which come within the purview of the Department of Marine and Fisheries and those which are generally understood to come within the meaning of the term ' natural resources,' and I trust therefore that when the House comes to determine what shall be the scope of the proposed committee, it will eliminate anything relating to Marine and Fisheries. However, I am sure that there will be no great difficulty on that score, and that the hon. leader of the opposition will concur in my suggestion. There is just one other matter which is recalled to my mind by the mention by my hon. friend of a lumber operator in Nova Scotia, Mr. Miller, who does a large business in the county of Halifax. Mr. Miller has carried on lumber operations in many European countries and takes a deep interest in the conservation of our Canadian forest resources. I remember his telling me personally, not so very long ago, that he imported from Scotland spruce tree seeds for the purpose of seeding a certain number of acres of his holdings in the county of Halifax each year. For the last three years, he has made it a practice to seed about fifty acres each year of the land he cut over the preceding year. Some two or three years ago he imported from Scotland a quantity of these spruce, seeds, naturally thinking he was doing some good to the country as well as advancing his own private interests, and being under the impression that these seeds were free of duty. You may imagine, Mr. Speaker, that he was rather mortified to find he was compelled to pay duty. The only suggestion I have to make is that the Minister of Customs should reduce his revenue tariff just a little bit by putting spruce seeds on the free list.
Parliament makes the law, and I only carry it out.
I would like to make a few observations regarding one matter which has attracted my attention for some years past. Whether the committee asked for, could, if appointed, do

I shall not, Mr. Speaker, take up much of the time of the House discussing this resolution. By the expression ' conservation and development of the natural resources

the work or not-and I do not think they could-it is very desirable to determine, at the earliest date, to whom these water-powers belong. Of late years a great many people are coming to this parliament to get incorporated for the purpose of controlling water-powers all over the country. We have had a Bill read the first time to-day for that purpose, and that is the same Bill which was thrown out last session by the Senate. It is quite clear to me that the desire of the incorporators is to get control of the water-powers of three important streams in the province of Ontario. Five or six years ago, I asked if the question had yet been determined as to whether these water-powers belonged to the provinces or to the Dominion. I can understand that the Dominion may control navigable streams, but many of these streams .are not navigable, and on some of the latter the most valuable water-powers are found. It is for the purpose of getting control of these water-powers and streams that these companies are being incorporated. Some four or five years ago I brought this matter up and asked the government to have the question determined by some tribunal so that we might know whether the control lay within the provinces or the Dominion. If the water-powers belong to the provinces, the provinces ought to have control, because these powers will be one of the most valuable provincial assets. If they belong to the federal authorities, let the federal authorities determine how they shall be controlled. But if there he a joint interest, let it be determined what belongs to the provinces and what to the federal authorities. But the question ought to be determined at the earliest possible moment. It is absolutely necessary that it should be in order to stop the efforts of individuals or corporations to get control. I hope the government will not forget this phase of the matter and endeavour to have the question settled at the earliest possible moment.

I am happy to say that I have no word of dissent to express regarding the principle involved in my hon. friend's motion. The government is prepared to accept it and indeed would be prepared at once to grant this motion but for a consideration which I shall present later on to my hon. friend. He has said that the tendency of the present age is towards the decadence of parliament. I am not prepared to agree with him on that point, though I admit that the tendency is rather to put more and more responsibility on the government. Formerly members of this House would take the responsibility of certain legislation, but it is now felt better to draw the attention to, or the government to, certain subjects and expect the government to take them up and carry them to a successful issue. This Mr. SPROULE.
motion is somewhat at variance with the principles of parliamentary government as they came to us in 1867. We have several committees in this House, but all are intended for the one purpose only, namely, to aid legislation. We have the Committee on Railways to which all questions affecting railways are referred. We have the Committee on Banking and Commerce to which commercial questions are referred. We have the Committee on Private Bills to which is referred measures that do not affect railways or public works or banking. We have also the Committee on Agriculture, but that is a departure from the accepted doctrine which prevailed in 1867 when we got our constitution. That committee is not an aid towards legislation.
It is a committee of general information. And the work which has been done by that committee cannot be too highly praised. It has, almost every year, brought valuable suggestions to the attention of the House, and it has been the leader in legislation which has been most useful to the country. It has not initiated legislation itself-it could not do that,-but it has brought to the attention of the House from time to time important suggestions which the country demanded. The suggestion of my hon friend for a committee on natural resources is in the line, as he has said, of the Committee on Agriculture. It is not, as I have said, according to my reading of parliamentary institutions, as they have been. But parliamentary institutions must move with the times. I think the suggestion of my hon. friend is a good one. But I have one observation to offer, and one which I will ask him to consider between now and the time when this debate is resumed-as I intend to propose in a moment that it should be adjourned for the present. He has included in the work of his proposed committee a very wide sphere of action. He proposes that this committee should deal with fisheries, forests, mines, minerals, waterways and water-powers. A committee of that kind, it seems to me, would be cumbrous. He has suggested that the committee might divide" itself into sub-committees. I would suggest that it would be more in accordance even with the object he has in mind to make, not one committee only, but several committees. Exception has been taken by my hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. A. K. Maclean) to the inclusion of fisheries in the work of this committee; he suggests that a committee should be appointed to deal with this subject alone. I agree with my hon. friend from Lunenburg, and also with my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) who moved a resolution last year, and has repeated it this year, that the fisheries should be the subject of a committee by itself. We might deal with the subject of fisheries as we have dealt with the subject of agricul-

ture. Next, mines might very well be made the subject of one committee's operations, as agriculture has been and fisheries would be. I think we might also have a special committee for forests. Possibly, there might be another for waterways. But forests and waterways are so intimately connected that, perhaps, they might be made the subject of one committee. I think we will all agree in what has been shown by the expert opinion quoted by my hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden) in his very interesting speech that, if we wish to preserve our waterways, we must preserve our forests. If our land is denuded of its forest cover the country must pay the penalty of ruined waterways. As these two naturally go together, we might give one committee charge of forests and waterways.
And water-powers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: And water-powers. I would observe that it might be better for the general convenience of the House if we had more committees with less numerous membership. Our committees, at present, are unwieldy. The activity of members seeks exercise in some way, and all desire to be on committees. If, instead of six or seven committees, we have more, we might reduce the membership of the committees and engage the activity of members dealing with important subjects of which those committees would have charge. So, as I have suggested, we might have a committee on fisheries, a committee-already established-on agriculture, a committee on mines, a committee on forests and waterways-or, possibly, one on forests and one on waterways; as to that, I would not give a definite opinion, but we invite the opinion of the House. If these views are in accord with the general object which my hon. friend wishes to attain, I think I would be prepared to agree with him altogether. My only suggestion, as I have said, is that, instead of having one committee as is proposed by my hon. friend, we should appoint several committees. I will not press the matter, but will move the adjournment of the debate so that my hon. friend may consider the suggestions I have made.

So far as I am concerned, I would be prepared to fall in with the suggestions of the Prime Minister I can see no possible objection to the appointment of several committees; in fact, I might have made the motion in that way, but one naturally felt that it would be a rather startling proposal that four or five new committees should be appointed, and that it would be better to begin by proposing one. No doubt, the work would be better done in the way the Prime Minister has suggested.
Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.

LANCASTER (Lincoln and Niagara) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 6) to amend the Railway Act. He said:	Perhaps the Prime Minister would
like a word or two of explanation, but he will hardly desire more, as this is a well-known Bill. It has been discussed in this House for five years. After three years' discussion, it was passed by the House unanimously exactly in the form in which it is now, and for the last three sessions it has been passed by this House in that form and rejected by the Senate. The Bill is designed to provide for the protection of the public at railway level crossings in cities, towns and villages. I should think it would suffice to point out, as I have already done, that the Bill exactly as it is now, and after a full consideration, has been passed by this House. I may say that it was amended to its present form when the present member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) was Minister of Railways and Canals. It was the subject of consideration by a special committee, where it was discussed for days and days, and where all that the railways had to say upon it-which was a great deal-was heard and voluminous evidence taken. The Bill was reported to the House unanimously by the special committee, and was unanimously passed by this House and sent to the Senate. Towards the end of the session of 1906 it went to the Senate, and naturally, one would think, without my making that remark, that it might have had some attention when it went there. I wish to point out to the House that it went to the Senate very late, because a committee of this chamber had spent a good deal of time during the session in getting it into that form, and it was not considered nossible by the Senate to deal with it then. But the next session previous to the last session, when the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) was Minister of Railways and Canals, it was passed unanimously by this House, and again last session. Therefore I think I can well ask this House, without going into a long discussion of the Bill, and in view of the great number of accidents that are happening at this time, to confirm the action of this parliament the last two sessions, and send this Bill, which is exactly in the same form, again to the Senate for their consideration this session.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The last House has expressed its opinion of this Bill of my hon. friend, and I do not think that the old members would be inclined to revise their opinion. Therefore, unless some of the new members find it unsatisfactory, and unless we hear from them, I think the mo-| tion ought to be carried.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. P. BRODEUR (Minister of Marine and Fisheries).

The hon. gentleman was not on the special committee that dealt with that subject. We dealt with the suggestion of the then Minister of Railways, and I fell in with it. The railways complained that they would be put to an unnecessary expense if they had to deal with a lot of crossings which years ago had been ordered to be protected by the Railway Committee of the Privy Council. The court is extinct, but the judgments remain, that is, the court has ceased to exist-I call it a court, to use simpler language. The Railway Committee of the Privy Council, years ago, gave orders in regard to certain of these crossings, and the railways contended before the committee that or if we referred this question only to the Railway Commission they would be obliged to go to elaborate expenses, to call witnesses, to take levels by engineering experts, and so on, and that a great many of these protections already ordered might well stand until the commission saw fit, for some reason, to change them. speechtext:
CLARKE (South Essex) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 7) to amend the Railway Act. He said: The object of the amendment which I propose is to enlarge the classes of property for which a railway company shall be liable in case of fire communicated by a railway locomotive. In 1903, section 298, as it is at present in the Revised Statutes of Canada, was enacted. That provided that whenever damage should be caused to crops, lands, fences, plantations, or buildings and their contents, by a fire started by a railway locomotive, the company should be liable for damage so caused, with a provision limiting the amount of such damage in case the railway company could show that it was not guilty of any negligence. The object of the present amendment is to strike out the words which specify the kinds of property to which damage may be caused and for which the railway company is responsible. You will notice by section 298 that it is con-Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
fined to crops, lands, fences, plantations, or buildings and their contents. Now, it has been found in the experience of people owning property adjacent to railways, that there are other classes of property which are not enumerated in this section; for instance, building material. If a house is set on fire a railway company is liable under this section; if the house is not erected, the lumber, shingles and other materials upon the ground are not covered by this section. Another class of property which frequently suffers, in my constituency particularly, is cordwood and bolts for staves ; if they are destroyed, they do not come within this section.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT-FIRE CAUSED BY LOCOMOTIVES.
speechtext: And fence rails not yet put up into fences.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT-FIRE CAUSED BY LOCOMOTIVES.
speechtext:
A case has arisen in the courts of Ontario in regard to marsh hay which has been baled. The contention has already been set up that this does not come within the definition of crops, and the courts held that it does. But the case is still subject to appeal, the words are capable of some misconstruction. I therefore move that these words be struck out, and that the section as amended shall read as follows:
Whenever damage is caused by a fire started by a railway locomotive, the company making use of such locomotive, whether guilty of negligence or not, shall be liable to such damage.
So whatever property is damaged, the company will be liable for such damage. The section was introduced last year by the then member for New Westminster and was referred to the Railway Committee, and passed in almost the very words of the Bill I am now proposing. The only difference was that instead of leaving the question of liability entirely at large the Railway Committee inserted words making it read 'damage to any property.' I have no particular objection if the House thinks it proper to add these words, but I would prefer to have them omitted. For instance, damage might be caused to a human being, a house might be set on fire and the inmates injured. But if it were limited to property there would be no liability in that case. It seems to me there is as much reason to make it apply to injury to human beings or, say, to live stock, as to property, and, as it has been fully considered by the Railway Committee, I think the House might pass it through the Committee of the Whole without sending it to the Railway Committee.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT-FIRE CAUSED BY LOCOMOTIVES.

I know that in my constituency a man spent a considerable amount of money in planting out trees around his farm. A railway set fire to the prairie and destroyed the trees to the value of a couple of hundred dollars, and he had no redress whatever. If this Bill is passed it should cover any such cases.

speakeroldname: Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT-FIRE CAUSED BY LOCOMOTIVES.
speechtext: This Bill, while not lengthy, is very wide in its scope. I know that last session, even before it got before the committee, it was the subject of private consultation, and it was agreed by every person that the Act as it now stands is not satisfactory, that it is too circumscribed, and that when any damage occurs it is a matter of practice at least that the railways take the exception that the property destroyed does not come within the terms of the Act. If my hon. friend who has introduced the Bill wishes to put it into the form of last year I have no objection to proceeding with it ; if not, we should send it to the Railway Committee. maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT-FIRE CAUSED BY LOCOMOTIVES.
