Then there is the assistant clerk of the Privy Council, whose salary was $2,100 and who is now receiving $2,850 under the last Act. All the other increases are simply statutory. There have been five messengers for the last twenty years, but three were paid out of contingencies and have now been transferred to the Civil Service list. The contingencies for printing and stationery have been increased $400. We have dropped altogether the clerical and other assistants. The messenger's estimate, which was paid out of the regular items, were formally paid out of this vote for contingencies. There is a decrease there of $3,000.
Department of Marine and Fisheries-Salaries, Professor E. E. Prince at $4,000, $228,640.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. P. BEODEUE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries).
speechtext:
The reasons for the increase are these:	There were several
officers who were not included in the inside service, but in view of the change of the law last session they have been transferred to the inside service. The deputy minister has had his salary increased from $4,000 to $5,000 by the law of last session. Professor Prince has been appointed Canadian commissioner under the treaty passed with the United States. His salary before was $2,500 and in view of his appointment as treaty commissioner we have raised his salary to $4,000 in order to put him on the same footing as the American commissioner. By the treaty it is provided that two commissioners

have to be appointed for the purpose of drafting regulations. One is appointed by the American authorities and the other by the Canadian or British authorities.
For what term is he appointed?
For four years, if I remember right. The regulations which have to be made will have to be made for four years.
Will this commission trnve any jurisdiction over our inland fisheries, say, on Lake Ontario?

The treaty covers Pas-samaquoddy bay, the St. Croix river and two lakes in the province of Quebec, also the River St. Lawrence where it forms the boundry line and the great lakes. Lake Ontario is included.

The western end of Lake Ontario from the Niagara river is not a boundary line, but is Canadian on both sides, and the people there are much alarmed lest this treaty may destroy the fishing industry entirely. What have the Americans to do with regulating the fisheries in a section such as that?

The situation is absolutely the same as in the case of Lake Superior. Although the western part is entirely within American territory it has been found ad visable that the whole lake should be included. This treaty will not have the effect of destroying the fisheries, but quite the reverse._ Those who have studied the subject claim that for years the fisheries were more or less destroyed owing to the fact that there were no regulations or that the regulations were not similar. On the American side there were three or four authorities making regulations on the same lake, which were all dissimilar and it was found advisable that they should be uniform. And the result will be, certainly, instead of destroying the fisheries, to protect the fisheries. That is the object that both British and American representatives had in view when the treaty was passed.

I see that the minister is more familiar with the facts than I am, but I am informed that in the western portion of Lake Ontario, which has Canada for its southern as well as its northern boundary,-I mean that portion of the lake opposite the county I have the honour to represent,-there is an important fishery, the cisco herring fishery. I am informed that the licenses, this year, will have a condition _ compelling the fishermen to use nets with a mesh of 2f inches. For the last fourteen years, they have been fishing with a mesh of 2f inches. If they are compelled to use a larger mesh, the effect will be to prohibit them from fishing, for they cannot catch these fish with this
class of net. What they fear is that this regulation which has been given out will be confirmed by this new commission or under this new treaty, and they are seriously alarmed for their industry. I trust the minister will bear in mind the peculiarity of the fishery of that section of the lake. I may tell him that the officer whose salary we are now discussing is quite familiar with the cisco fishery and with the class of fish found in that part of the lake. All I ask is that these people should be protected. Their all is bound up in this fishing industry. There is no use of saying that the fishing is being destroyed. The fish there were as abundant last year as they ever were. That is the information I have. I was there during the autumn, and there is no complaint that the fish are being depleted, in fact, the fishing last season was excellent. But if the fishermen are compelled to use the larger mesh, it will make no difference whether the fish are plentiful or scarce. The fish do not grow large, but those that would -be caught with the larger nets would be the mother fish, the breeders. I understand that a petition has been sent to the minister very recently. On inquiry on Saturday, I learned that it had not reached him then, but when it does reach him, I hope he will give it his serious consideration and will not allow the larger mesh to be made obligatory under the regulations.

I am under the impression that no change has been made in the regulations governing the fisheries in that part of Lake Ontario. Had any such regulations been passed, I should certainly have had knowledge of the fact, and I think I should have remembered it, but I have no recollection of any such change. The other regulations are not in force, they are not even drafted. But the two commissioners have been appointed under the treaty, as I have said, to draft these regulations. I will bring the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) to the attention of Prof. Prince, and will see to it that the fishermen are properly treated.

I am under obligation to the hon- minister for what he has said. My information comes direct from men engaged in the fisheries, and I understand they get their information from Mr. Tinsley, of Toronto, who, I presume, does not speak without the authority of the minister, for he knows perfectly well that, while he has to do with the licensing of the fishermen, no change in the regulations can be made without the consent of the minister. I hope the minister will stand firm in the interest of the fishermen, and that he will consult his officers and any one else who can give him information on the subject. I feel sure 'that if he does this he will not permit any change in the regulations that have been in existence during the last fourteen or fifteen years.

Of course, I am speaking subject to correction on this subject. But I have been giving the matter great consideration and study recently, and I feel sure that any such change in the regulations would have been impressed upon my memory. I certainly have no recollection of such a change having been made.

I would suggest that this item be allowed to stand. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) is not here, neither is the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden). This item is increased this year from about $115,000 to about $228,000, a very large increase and one that calls for explanation. There are a number of items that are non-contentious, such as items 10, 11, 12, 21, 23, 25 and 26. These,
I think, we might dispose of.

I have no objection to allowing the item to stand, but I would not like these figures to be considered as representing an increase in the export on the fisheries. There have been a few increases, but the figures just read do not explain the situation. The hon. gentleman will see that the figure for last year, $115,250, represents the salaries voted under Civil Government last year. But by virtue of the law passed last session, all the officers in the fisheries branch in Ottawa, some of whom were paid out of the different votes, are now to be paid out of the Civil Government vote.

I understand that. But I find, at page 24, that the number of officers last year was 78 temporary and 77 permanent, a total of 155. Now, there are 171, a very considerable increase. I am sure that the number now is double what it was in 1896, though the work is practically the same.
Oh, no.

I would ask that this item be allowed to stand until the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr Foster), who was at one time Minister of Marine and Fisheries, is present.
Office of the Auditor General-Contingencies $t),500.
There is a decrease here of $11,500, but I see that $11,000 is transferred to salaries.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Exactly.
Carried.

The Chairman must take into consideration the fact that we only had these estimates placed in our hands a short time before the House rose at six o'clock. We have had no opportunity of looking at them, and I trust he will not cry ' Carried ' too soon. We are handling a good deal of money.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There is really not much money handled under this item Mr. HENDERSON.
The regular service last year was $71,000, this year it is $88,000. The contingencies were $18,000 last year, and $6,500 this year. The figures total about the same as last year.
Department of Finance and Treasury Board -Salaries, $107,812.50; Contingencies, $11,000.

I notice in this item that a third division, subdivision B, appears to be added this year that was not on before, and apparently 43 persons are taken in from the outside service. Is the cost increased?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes. The regular vote for contingencies last year was, in round numbers, $70,000, this year ^ is $107,000. This increase is explained by the fact that some 43 employees were taken from the outside service and put in the inside service.
I presume there will be 43 fewer people in the outside service than there were before?
What is the object of bringing them in from the outside service?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As provided by the Act of last year.
It appears that a great many of these men are to have their salary increased by $150; is that in addition to this vote?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
So that what we are voting now as salaries to these men is not what they are to be paid. A considerable number of them are to be paid $150 each more than is put in the estimates.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
That is a serious matter to take into consideration. The salaries here are very much the same as they were last year.
With the statutory allowances.

What about them?
Are we ever to hear anything more about them? Are they to drop out of sight?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There will be statutory increases every year until a civil servant reaches the maximum of his class. The allowance increases from year to year by $50 until he has reached the maximum of the class he belongs to.

I was in hopes that we had got this Civil Service matter about where we could comprehend it. It seems to me the First Minister has not simplified the matter at all. He is going to add $150 to the salaries of a certain number of men, not all the men. Then some men, we do net know how many, we do not know who

they are, are to have their salaries increased year by year by $50. Now, if the Prime Minister could appoint a committee of this House to make the matter a little more obtuse than it is, I would like to see them at work.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am quite
willing to take the suggestion of my hon. friend. I have been some thirty years in the House, and I cannot say that I understand the Civil Service Act yet.
How many civil servants are now at the maximum of their various classes?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I cannot say.

There is another question. A civil servant will get his $150 added this year, for I suppose the government intends to put that Bill through. Will that do in lieu of three years of statutory increase, or is the statutory increase to be over and above the $150.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is.

That is a big lump. That means that each one will get $200 this year of an increase, at least a great many of the men. The impression has gone abroad in the country that all they were getting was $150 each, and that that was a settlement of the whole account. I do not know whether the First Minister, during the election promised more than that or not, I think it was only $150 each that was promised. But now it seems it is getting worse and worse; the increase is more than he promised.
Department of Trade and Commerce-Salaries, $38,837.50; contingencies, $19,350.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am satisfied there are no increases except those authorized last year by the Civil Service Act, except the annuities branch, which is a new branch altogether.
Does the Prime Minister think it necessary to continue this branch or has he any thought of abolishing it as recommended by the minister who presided over it a few years ago ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Far from it, it is more useful than ever.
Office of the High Commissioner for Canada in London, salaries, $10,600.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is no increase there except what is authorized by the statute of last year.
W7ho is the secretary referred to there ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Griffith.

That increase of $200 to the assistant secretary has no relation to 13
the $150 or the statutory increase, that is only an additional sum given to him ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
The next one has an increase of $100. I find there are a great many increases outside the statutory increases of $150. There seems to be an increase all along the line.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
These increases were authorized by the statute of last session.
High commissioner's office, London, contingencies, $19,775.

Would the minister say how that compares with say 15 years ago ? Away back in the 90's we heard a good deal about the expenses of the London office. Are we doing the work there as reasonably as it was done then or are we getting a little more extravagant in England as we are in Canada ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I was in the House at that lime, 15 years ago and I never heard my hon. friend complain that we were extravagant in those days.

I never complain, but I heard the right hon. the Prime Minister and his friends complain by the hour, denouncing the extravagance of the London office. I am afraid they have forgotten their virtue of those days. I do not know that we have any better service than we had 15 years ago.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We have a very good service.

I called at the London office about two years ago and I tell you I would not give Mr. Griffith $5,000 for
his services. I have not a very high estimate of the way he treats strangers, much less members of parliament. I do not care if he reads that in ' Hansard.'
Has the Prime Minister any information as to the amount of the income tax on the salary of the High Commissioner?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I shall obtain the information at a later date.
Office of general consulting engineer to Dominion government, salaries, $7,250.
When Mr. Schreiber acts as arbitrator as I understand he is doing on the present occasion to settle differences between the Grand Trunk Pacific and the government, is he paid extra ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not think so, it is not so intended.
Civil Service Commission, salaries, $19,075.
W'hen did the Civil Service Commissioners definitely take office and commence work ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think they were appointed on the 1st of September. I cannot say exactly when they took office but about that time, in September.

Who are the
commissioners ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Professor Shortt and Mr. Larochelle of Montreal.
Would the Prime Minister be good enough to state in very brief detail what the duties of these men are ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It would be difficult to put their duties into brief words. The duties of the commissioners are being defined by themselves now, they are establishing rules for the carrying on of their work. As my hon. friend knows, their chief duty is to select officers for the recruiting of the Civil Service. We have no power at the present time to appoint anybody to the service. For instance, the Minister of Customs would have to write to the Civil Service Commissioners that there is a vacancy of a certain character in his department and asking the commissioners to supply an officer, and the commissioners would appoint the successful competitor in the examination.
Do the commissioners select the man who has the highest marks?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think so. I cannot say they do it mechanically, but the theory of the' Act is that the successful competitor shall be appointed.

And would the Civil Service Commissioners have a right to reply to the Minister of Customs, saying:	You
have a sufficient staff already; you do not need another man and we will not let you appoint one. I for one am desirous that the inside and outside service should be well paid. I much prefer they should be well paid than that they should be underpaid. I have said before, and I say again, that in the Civil Service we have a great many educated men, men of ability, and men who are most accommodating and obliging when you meet them, but I do believe that the inside service is overmanned. I have the idea, I may be wrong, that you could dismiss from the service 500 officials and still have enough to do the work. I do not ask that any of these officials should be dismissed, because it would be a hardship, but I do think that when a vacancy occurs that vacancy should not be filled until there is a most careful inquiry as to whether there are not already sufficient employees to discharge the duties of any given department. I would have the officials work longer hours; I do not think there is any difficulty in an able-bodied man, or woman either, working six hours a day. Why, in my youth Mr. AMES.
I used to work twelve and fifteen hours a day and think nothing of it, but now a man gets fatigued after five or six hours work and he has to get out and play lawn tennis to recuperate his health, and we provide him with grounds for that purpose. I do not find fault with that, because that is probably as good a way as any other to occupy one's leisure time. But I do press on the government that a general opinion prevails in this House and outside of it that the service in Ottawa is overmanned. I am told that there are men in the service today whose time is largely taken up in simply revising the work of others who have not acquired a competent knowledge of their duties, and that these men who do know their business would be quite sufficient to do all the work that the service calls for. I would not advise the government to do any wholesale weeding out, because, as I have said, it would be a hardship to dismiss these employees, but if vacancies were not filled except in cases where it was absolutely necessary to do so, in eight or ten years you would be astonished to find how much fewer officials you could get along with. Then I would be in favour of the principle that those who remain in the service should get increased pay so as to encourage them in an energetic discharge of their duties. I am sure the work of the departments could be better done under such a system than by bringing in new men every six months, or every month or every day for that matter and schooling them in their duties. I do not look for so very much from this new system of appointing civil servants. The First Minister may knit his eyebrows; perhaps he realizes that the old system of pull would be better. By this competitive examination system you may get a man well up in algebra or Euclid or English grammar, or he may be a university graduate, but he may not be worth a button when he comes to perform some minor duty in the department. I understand that the examination will only be along the ordinary lines as a test of education.
Oh, no.

Suppose you want an officer for the Customs Department, will he undergo an examination calculated to test his knowledge of the difference between cotton goods and woollen goods so that he may be able to determine the duty which should be paid? If that were so, then you would want to have as many commissioners as there are departments; you would want a man for the Fishery Department who would be able to conduct an examination as to the quality of the nets and the size of the mesh that would catch a big fish or a small fish, and you would want another for the Militia Department which would be

able to decide on what were the qualifications for a soldier. I have no hope that this commission is going to accomplish what we anticipate for it. I believe we will find that in the end pull will have as much to do with it as anything else. At all events I would urge on the government that vacancies should not be filled unless it is absolutely necessary to fill them, and if you have $347,000 additional to give to the civil servants I would divide part of that amongst the officers who remain in the service, weeding out the surplusage as vacancies occur and paying better the men who remain. If this were done, I am sure you would have more satisfaction amongst the civil servants of the country. Then when I and others go to the different departments we shall find the officials thoroughly posted in their work and prepared to give us the information we desire instead of meeting a young man who, from no fault of his own, is utterly unacquainted with the business he is assuming, and will perhaps be out of the office again in six months or a year and a new man put in his place. I trust the government will take up my idea and think over it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am very much disappointed at the remarks of my hon. friend. I thought he would give us some encomium for what we have done, but instead of that he gives us a lot of blame. My hon. friend, after paying a graceful compliment to the Civil Service, went on to say that it was largely composed of men who could not do their work and whose work had to be supervised by other officers; and he suggests that when vacancies occur we should not fill them. Well, if vacancies occurred in the offices of some of the good men who do the supervising, and the service were left to the incompetent ones, what would become of it? My hon. friend will see that the best course is to go on and apply the law as we have it, making appointments by competition and not by pull, as my hon. friend thinks is the case now. That is one of the prejudices of the other side. In order to satisfy the fastidiousness of my hon. friend we passed the present law, under which we have no pull. All the pull is with the commissioners, who I am sure are impartial ; and I am sure that under the operation of the law we shall have a good service, every man doing good work without his work requiring to be supervised by any other man.

Of course, my remarks could not apply to every one in the Civil Service. No civil servant will take exception to them in that respect, because no one could expect a man who has been in the service only six months to be as competent as those who have been there for six years. You find in the service a 131
great many men who are well up in their work and always accommodating and obliging. These are deserving men whom I want to see well paid. The First Minister asks what we would do when one of these good men drops out. I think the best thing would be to promote the next man below him. In that way you will fill the bill better than by appointing a raw recruit.
Who determines the appointments in the different departments- the minister or the Civil Service Commission?

The Act provides that officers requiring technical or professional knowledge may be appointed otherwise, but the great bulk of the appointments to the Civil Service are by competitive examination. For example, a clerk in the cheque branch of the Customs Department dies, and the Commissioner of Customs reported to me that it was necessary to fill the vacancy. Thereupon, as the Act provided, the Commissioner drew up a requisition to the Civil Service Commissioners to furnish us with an officer, and I as,minister wrote ' approved ' upon it. That requisition goes to the Civil Service Commission. They hold an examination, and we know nothing of the man they send us. I think they are using the old Civil Service examinations in a measure, but no doubt they will have new examinations before long. The young man who is sent to us was not known before either to my deputy or to myself, and he takes the position-not the position or the salary of the officer who died ; but we said to him, ' We have a vacancy in the cheque department, and we require one who writes a good hand, is good at figures and mathematics, and has a retentive 'memory.' We put him into the class in which the officer who died was placed in the reorganization of the service, not at $1,300, which I think he received, but at the minimum of the class.

Suppose there is a vacancy in the first class, do you make a new appointment to that class, or do you move one from the second class to the first and one from the third class to the second, and make a new appointment to the third class?
In this case it is done by placing the new officer at the minimum of the class to which he is appointed.
And all the others are passed up one grade accordingly?
No; their salaries remain as they were. They receive the statutory increase year by year, but a new man goes in at the minimum of the class.
Who fills the place of the first-class man who drops out? Is there a promotion made?
No, there is no promotion made in that case.
Who determines whether the department is over-manned or not -the minister or the commission?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If a new appointment is to be made, the government must come to parliament for an appropriation, and then the appointment is made in the way stated by my hon. friend.

I wish to make a few observations in regard to the inconvenience to which members of parliament are frequently put in trying to do business with the departments. The present custom is for a portion of the service to leave their offices for lunch from twelve to one o'clock, and another portion from one to two o'clock. We usually come here between nine and ten in the morning to get our mail, and after we get through with that there may or may not be committee work, and then it is pretty near twelve o'clock. If we go to the departments to-day to do any business, as a general thing, we are met with the answer that the clerk in charge of that branch is away at lunch and will not be back until one and we cannot very well get the papers ? We go back after one o'clock and we find that the head of the branch is at lunch and will not be back until two. There are thus two hours in which we cannot do any work. It would be a much better system for all officers to leave for lunch at twelve and be back at one or leave at one and be back at two. You go there at two o'clock and often they are not back and you have to wait until nearly three when you have to go to the House, and by the time the routine business of the House is done the offices are closed. Then on Saturday, these members who do not leave the city make an effort to overtake their accumulated work, the morning is usually taken up with routine work of mails, until it is noon, then at one o'clock the departments are closed and the whole afternoon you can do nothing. That is the experience of most members who have been here any length of time. Some change should be made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am sure that there has been no change in the service in my experience but I shall speak to my colleagues about my hon. friend's suggestion.

A few years ago this question was. brought up and it was then intimated that a large number of the junior clerks might have their lunch hour from twelve to one or from one to two, and the senior officers either from twelve to one or from one to two. At present it happens that just when you want to do business, you cannot get any one to do it.
Under what department or minister does this Civil Service Commission fall ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is like the Auditor General absolutely independent of the ministers.
Will there be a detailed report each year ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

I do not want to find fault, but in any industry in this country the employees generally work from at least eight in the morning until six in the evening, I do not know what the particular hours are for the civil servants, but at the very best they are no longer than from 9.30 a.m. until 4 p.m. I have gone to the offices and have found that even at 10 a.m. the officials are often not there. I do not think it would be a great hardship upon the officials if they went to work a little earlier in the morning and quit work a little later in the afternoon. If that were done, we could dispense with a good many of them. Any man in this country should be able to work from 8 a.m. until noon and then from one until 5 p,m. Let the right hon. the Prime Minister inquire of any manufacturer whether his employees do not work from 8 a.m. until 6 p.m.; I believe that the ministers themselves and their deputies are there from at least 9 a.m. until 6 p.m.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: And later.

Yes later. I honestly believe that an employee in the service at Ottawa should work from 9 a.m. until 5 or 5.30 p.m. And if they did we could dispense with quite a number. I agree with what my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has said, that it was almost impossible to do anything in the departments for this reason. You go there at ten a.m. and find a lot of people waiting to do business before you, and by the time your turn has come, the officials go to lunch. Then by the time you can get back after lunch, the office is closed. Is it unreasonable to ask that these men should be on duty from nine till twelve and from one till five, or seven hours per day. I have been told by an ex-official, and one of the best, that as a rule the officers only get there about ten o'cleck, then they go away at twelve or one, and at four o'clock they are gone again. This man was always there at nine sharp and worked until six and was glad to do it, as he could get through Ills work more satisfactorily in that way. I do not wish to impose any hardships, but I believe that any man who accepts a position in a government department should be there at nine a.m., take an hour for his lunch, and then remain until 5.30. If that were done, we could do with a good many less officials.
It is rather interesting to listen to my hon. friends. For years when the Conservatives were in power, exactly the same conditions existed and we never heard from them a word of protest.

The hon. gentleman is
mistaken.

I would like the member from East Grey to point to me one utterance of his criticising the civil servants for not being in their departments during every hour of the day, while the Conservatives were in power.
I do not wonder that my hon. friend did not hear me because he was so seldom here, but I have made the same criticism on numerous occasions and can turn to ' Hansard ' to prove my words.

I could not possibly keep track of everything the hon. gentleman has said because he has so much to say on everything. But I have had as much to do with the civil servants, in at any rate three of the departments, as any other member of parliament for the last twenty, years, and I will say this. Take the Department of Railways and Canals and the Public Works Department and the Department of Marine and Fisheries, which has been so much talked about, there has not been an hour in the day from ten a.m. until six p.m. when you could not find one of the leading officers" there to do business with.
You are an exception; they favour you.

I believe I am not an exception. They were there when the Conservatives were in power, and they are there now. The chief officers of this department are in their offices from ten in the morning to six at night, with an hour for lunch.
That is what I admitted.

Then I cannot see what the hon. gentleman has to complain of. Surely, with these hours, they are performing their duties. Most of these officers having been appointed years ago are probably Conservatives in politics. But I believe that the public servants of this government are as fine a body as can be found in this or any other country. They are attentive and faithful in the performance of the services for which they are paid. They are intelligent and accommodating, and will grant any favour that is in their power. Why any hon. member of this House should complain of them I cannot understand, unless it is that my hon. friends opposite want to get some of their own friends into office. I am not sure that I am in favour of the Civil Service Commission. If I were a minister of the Crown I would appoint my own officers, and would not want
the Civil Service Commission to appoint them for me. I would select them myself, and I would select good ones, and I would have a body of officers that, I am sure, would satisfy even my hon. friend from Grenville (Mr. J. D. Reid).

The hon. gentleman (Mr. German) tries to censure me because I did not complain of the hours of the Civil Service when the Conservatives were in power. I was then, of course, a new member. In the remarks I made I was not censuring this government in particular, Even though the hours are the same now as when the Conservatives were in power, is that any reason why, if I should think the hours should be longer so as to reduce the number of employees, I should not mention it at this time? The hon. member for Welland states that the deputies, or a few of the leading officials, are in their departments until six o'clock at night. I admit that you can go there at that hour and find, probably, the deputy minister and his secretary, or the minister and his secretary, and perhaps the chief clerk. But 95 per cent of the officials have gone, having left as soon as the clock struck four. If the deputy and private secretary and the minister can work, as I believe many of them do, from nine o'clock until six every day, and probably long after that, why should not the other officials do the same? A clerk in the Civil Service should perform as many hours as he would in any manufacturing concern. I may be wrong in that opinion, but I hold that opinion until I am proven wrong. I contend that the officials here would not be overworked if their hours were from 9 o'clock in the morning until 5 or 5.30 in the afternoon. I believe that such a rule would help the minister and the deputy. When these leaders in the department remain late, they must require papers from the different rooms, and if officials were there they could supply them. And, if the hours were extended, is it not reasonable to expect that fewer clerks would be required to do the work? I am not finding the slightest fault with the members of the Civil Service. I admit that we have a good service; the officers are accommodating and willing to do anything they can to assist one who has to do business with them. All I say is that if the hours were made what seems to me reasonable hours, fewer clerks would be required to do the work. But so long as the law is that the officers can go at four o'clock
There is no law to that effect. The clerks of the Public Works Department do not leave until 4.30.

Well, even admitting that it is 4.30 o'clock, it strikes me that that is rather early in the day for the officials to leave. I venture to say that

396'
there are many men in this House who employ large staffs of clerks, and I would like any one of these to say if he makes the hours for his staff from 9 to 4 or 4.30. You will find that, as a rule, the hours are from 8 in the morning till 6 at night, and many of them even come back after six o'clock. I believe that if the departments were open from 9 a.m. to 5 or 5.30, one-third of the civil servants would not be required. I say that without any disrespect to the members of the Civil Service.

The hon. member (Mr. J. D. Reid) is not altogether right as to the number of hours civil servants work. I have had some experience in the Department of the Interior. The clerks of that department must be in attendance by 9.30 in the morning. They have to sign a book. At 9.30 a line is drawn and the book is taken into the deputy minister's office and any who arrive after that time are noted as being late. They get an hour and a half, not two hours, for lunch, and they sign the book when they go out and when they return as well. In the Department of the Interior the clerks work until 4.30 p.m. in the summer and during the winter until 5 o'clock. I know that is not the rule in some of the departments, but in the Department of the Interior these are the hours. As pointed out by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) the deputy ministers and many of the chief clerks are at work at 9 a.m. and remain in their office until half past five or six p.m. I agree with some of the remarks that have been made on this subject, that those clerks who reach the office at half past nine o'clock and scarcely get to work before ten, and leave at four in the afternoon, are not doing a proper day's work. I think there ought to be a uniform regulation made by which the hours of service in all the departments at Ottawa should be of the same length, and it would do no harm if they were made to last till five in the afternoon the year round.

It seems to me the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) has put up a few straw men for the sake of knocking them down. I am sure he defended a great many things which have not been attacked. The hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Reid) spoke of appointing fewer men and giving them longer hours. I have felt ever since I have been a member of this House, while not wishing by any means to ask anything unreasonable from the civil servants, that the hours they work are too short. Whatever the .law may be, it is the practice that we have to deal with; and the practice is, notwithstanding the remarks of my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), that the great proportion of the civil servants leave their offices at four o'clock in the afternoon. I may mention an Mr. J. D. REID.
illustration that came to my notice yesterday, showing the effect of short hours. A young man told me that he was formerly in the Civil Service and I asked him why he left it. One reason he gave me was this: he said, because, when my duties are over at four o'clock in the afternoon, I have too much time on my hands. I believe there is a good deal in that. The young man and the young woman who get out at _ four o'clock have too much time for mischief.

In view of the observations of the hon. mfember for Welland (Mr. German) I wish to say that I neither intended to, nor did I reflect in any way on the civil servants. I do not hold them responsible for this arrangement, because I understood it was made by the deputy ministers in concurrence with the ministers, that a proportion of the employees should go away between 12 and 1 for lunch, and another portion between 1 and 2. I do not blame them at all, nor do I insinuate that they -were wanting in intelligence, in courtesy or in diligence. I said nothing about that at all, because I found them to be the reverse, in my experience. I was speaking about the inconvenience of the present system.

I would like to say a few words on this subject, as one who for many years has had a good deal to do with the various departments of the government. I am glad to hear my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) speaking for the. Interior Department. In my experience, while the hours named have been from 9.30 to 4.30, if you enter a department at any time before 6 o'clock, you will find in it a number of clerks still at work. While it may be said that from 9.30 to 4.30 are not long hours, it will be found throughout the country generally, if you take the practice in insurance companies, banking concerns, and others of a like nature, that the hours are no longer than from 9 until 4 o'clock, and in many cases until 3 o'clock. In my experience I have never known of any inconvenience or delay occurring in the different departments by reason of the hours of work ceasing at 4.30 in the afternoon. If there was work to be done after that hour, it was always done by a senior official or by a junior official. While a good deal has been said throughout the country about the duties of the civil servants, and some fun has been made of their short hours, I want to say now that this opinion is altogether unfounded. As I said the other day, any one acquainted with the different departments and the work as done in them will find, if he takes the trouble to ascertain, that the work is thoroughly well done during the present hours. We must not forget that long hours do not necessarily mean good work. When the work is being done as

satisfactorily as it is at present, I do not think the civil servants deserve some of the criticism that has been levelled against them.
Nobody has said the work was not well done.

I was glad to hear the honourable the junior member for Ottawa <Mr. McGiverin). I did not know that he had so much experience with the departments as to know how the work was being done. This is the first time I have heard that he was inspecting the departments to see what work was being done. We have never heard any of the ministers get up and make a statement such as we have just heard from the member for Ottawa, namely, that he knew that all the work was done at 4 o'clock or 4.30, and that if it was not, the officials stayed there longer. Now, I have it from an official, a gentleman who was high up in one of the departments, that the clerks do not get there until just before 9.30 in the morning, and at 4 o'clock in the afternoon 95 per cent of them walk out the minute the clock strikes 4, whether the work is done or not. If it is not done, they leave it until the next morning. This gentleman was high up in the department, he gave me this version of the case, and I *would prefer to accept his opinion to the opinion of the hon. member. The hon. gentleman suggests that in banks and other institutions the clerks do. not work any longer. But it is a well known fact that when a bank closes at 3 o'clock in the afternoon the clerks have to remain at least two hours afterwards to balance up their books, to write letters, and get things into shape. They go to work before 9 o'clock in the morning, and I have heard from managers of banks that it takes them two hours after the bank closes to finish up their work. They have only one hour for lunch. The hon. member for Assiniboia says that the hours in the departments are from 9.30 in the morning. They work for two hours and a half until 12 o'clock, then they have an hour and a half until 1.30 for lunch, then they work until 4.30 in the afternoon.
In summer, till 5 in the winter.

That is five hours and a half a day. Will any man .in the Dominion contend that five hours and a half is a day's work for any man in an office? The hon. member for Welland knows well enough, because I believe he is interested in some manufacturing industries, that if the clerks were not there at 8 o'clock in the morning and did not work till 6, he would dismiss them promptly. Here in Ottawa I think myself that the officials should commence at 9 o'clock and work till 5 or 5.30. I am not blaming this government any more
than their predecessors. It has been the rule probably ever since confederation. I claim that if the government would make the hours from 9 a.m. to 5.30 j).m. they would not require as many officials. People arriving here at 3.30 or 4 o'clock in the afternoon would be able to get work done and return home on the night trains. They cannot do this now on account of the short hours of the service.
Item allowed to stand.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The discussion recently has not been relevant to the question which is the Civil Service Commission; they have no power whatever over the hours of the Civil Service.

Are we to understand that the Commissioners have jurisdiction over or anything to do with the discipline of the employees of this House or are they simply appointed to ascertain the qualifications of the different candidates who apply for the Civil Service? Then what is understood by the distinction between the inside and the outside service? Are the officials of the Customs Department or the Militia or Public Works Department m Montreal or Toronto paid out of the appropriation for the inside service?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.
What about the discipline then?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have suggested that this item stand. A good deal of information has been asked for and can be given next time.

Before we leave the vote for Civil Government, would the Prime Minister explain whether the bringing in of the outside service to the inside service will account for the increase from $2,061,000 to $3 933,000? If you add to that the increase from $347,000, the increase being granted to the Civil Service you considerably more than double the amount of money that was given to them in 1908-9.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The outside service in Ottawa has been taken into the inside service and the salaries are now voted by parliament, whereas formerly they were voted in a lump sum in many departments. It is only a transferring of figures.
Would that be sufficient to double the amount?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is my impression, but I will have it. looked into.
Governor General's secretary's office, salaries $20,125.
What is the increase there?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
This is in consequence of the Act of last year. The only

large increase is that given to Sir John Hanbury-Williams. The intention was to bring his salary to the rank of subdivision A.
Would all that increase of nearly $9,000 be taken up by the increases of the three names mentioned here?
Five are brought in from the outside service.
What are the names ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I will get them later on.
Charges of management $303,200.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The only increases are from the outside service.
How do you make the large decrease?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I cannot answer that.
There is a decrease of $10,250.

I presume the explanation is that the $24,000 put in last year for the printing of Dominion notes is not in this year. Against that there are some increases amounting to some $8,000 altogether. One is an increase in the amount for the removal of foreign coin from circulation and about $2,000 in salaries' at Charlottetown, Winnipeg and Halifax.
.Mr. AMES. There is an item, 'Commission for payment of interest on public debt, purchase of sinking funds.' To whom is that commission paid?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I cannot give the explanation to my hon. friend this evening; I shall give it to-morrow.
Do I understand the First Minister will give a statement on that tomorrow?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Carried.

We have asked the item to stand on the promise of the First Minister that he would give us an explanation. We want to know all about this commission before the item passes. We do not expect that the right hon. gentleman would be in a position to answer the question to-night but the item should stand until we get the information.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My understanding was that the item should pass on the promise that I would give the explanation to-morrow.
My experience in this House is that when we let items go in this way they are never called again and we never get the explanation. The surest *way is to allow it to stand.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Very good.
That will be the rule for this session.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Oh, not this session ; just this time.
Item allowed to stand.
Some resolutions reported.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER moved the adjournment of the House.
What business does the government purpose taking up to-morrow ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The resolution of Mr. Fisher about the Civil Service ; then the estimates.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at ten p.m.
Tuesday, February 2, 1909.
